newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italian trade surplus could top 60 trln lire.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italian trade surplus could top 60 trln lire.

text.p: Italy's global trade surplus could exceed 60 trillion lire ($39.3 billion) in 1996, despite first signs that the country's export boom is finally fading, Foreign Trade Minister Augusto Fantozzi said on Friday.
The national statistics office Istat said Italy had a total trade surplus of 28.36 trillion lire in the first six months of the year, up 67.3 percent on the same period in 1995.
"In 1996 we may even exceed the optimistic target of a 60 trillion lire trade surplus," Fantozzi said.
"This positive outcome is due to a progressive slowdown in imports and a slight increase in exports...which are holding strong even if there are the first signs that they are slowing."
Italy had a total 1995 foreign trade surplus of 44.37 trillion lire as exports blossomed on the back of a sharp lira devaluation which made Italian products highly competitive on foreign markets.

"The surplus continues to widen even more than we had expected at the start of the year and we're approaching the moment when Italy will be able to wipe out its foreign debt built up in the 1980s," Fantozzi said.
More than 90 percent of Italy's huge debt mountain is lira-denominated.
Italy's trade surplus has been boosted by an unexpected drop in imports, reflecting the sluggish state of the economy.
Imports of goods from outside the European Union fell 6.4 percent in July against the same month in 1995, following a 17.9 percent drop in June, Istat figures showed.
Non-EU exports remained buoyant, surging 15.5 percent in July, year-on-year, despite a firmer lira.

However, recent strength of the lira has started to make itself felt on exports to countries within the European Union -- Italy's largest trading partner. Sales to EU states plunged 14.6 percent in June, Istat said on Friday.
Italy's economy grew three percent last year, boosted by the export boom.

The government had forecast a repeat performance in 1996, but economic slowdown elsewhere in Europe, coupled with the lira's gains and a tough Bank of Italy monetary policy have combined to depress gross domestic product (GDP).
Latest data showed Italy's GDP falling 0.5 percent between April and June compared with the first quarter of the year.

Most economists are now forecasting that the economy will grow by just 0.7 percent which could present the centre-left government with a headache as it tries to reach its 1996 financial targets and prepare the 1997 budget.
Falling GDP will inevitably hurt tax inflows and at the same time lead to more unemployment benefit payments, thereby jeopardising the government's public sector borrowing goals.

Earlier this week employers' federation Confindustria said Italy was heading for 125-130 trillion lire fiscal deficit in 1996 against a target 113 trillion lire, despite a government mini-budget in June aimed at keeping Italian accounts on track.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Friday urged people not to worry about the cries of alarm over the deficit. "Don't listen to the rumours. We produced a tough mini-budget and now we'll present a serious 1997 budget," he told reporters.
